‘418’ Movie Review: Chaitra J Achar Shines in a Promising but Half-Hearted Horror Saga

A Fresh Setting Meets Familiar Tropes

The Telugu horror film 418, backed by filmmaker Prashanth Neel and directed by his associate Kirtan Nadagouda, offers a striking initial setup that gradually loses steam. Moving away from the conventional haunted mansion, the movie establishes its eerie atmosphere in a boys’ hostel located in Vedagiri, Karnataka. The building formerly served as a mental asylum and sits on premises where local legend dictates that women are strictly barred. Set against the backdrop of 2020 and early COVID-19 fears, the narrative follows an introverted medical student, Vivek Shankar (played by Surya Raj Veerabathini), as he moves into a room adjacent to the titular, cursed Room 418.

Clocking in at a runtime of 148 minutes, the film features a cast that includes Chaithra J Achar, Preethi Pagadala, and Charan Lakkaraju. While the first half benefits from a raw, slow-burn anxiety, grainy visual textures, and imaginative editing transitions, the narrative eventually struggles to maintain its momentum.

Performances and Technical Craft

Critics highlight the technical merits of 418, particularly Dinesh Divakaran’s cinematography and Akul Avinash's editing, which help build early tension. Composer Venky GG and sound designer Anupam C also contribute heavily to the atmospheric mood, despite relying at times on standard jump scares.

Among the cast, Chaithra J Achar delivers a standout performance, using expressive eyes and external grace to mask her character's sinister ambitions. Surya Raj Veerabathini anchors the first half effectively as the nervy protagonist, while supporting performances by Preethi Pagadala, Charan Lakkaraju, Ramesh Indira, and Goparaju Vijay add freshness to the dynamic.

Analysis of Themes and Execution

The film attempts to weave social commentary into its supernatural plot, touching upon themes of caste, class discrimination, and internalised misogyny through the backstory of a female victim. Traditional elements like the yakshagana folk art form are used as an allegory to critique pressures surrounding motherhood. However, reviewers note that these promising thematic explorations ultimately resolve into a prolonged and ineffective finish, with the narrative faltering in its second half as it leans back into repetitive genre stereotypes.
